chapter: Early New Orleans and Plaquemine years
title: Concrete construction job in Algiers when music work failed
summary: With music slow, Love got a wheelbarrow job at $2.82 a day and was teased by the mixers.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: When I got to be a young man, when the music business failed on me, you know, there wasn't much to do, I come down here to learn more music and work on the first building to put that media down. Over here in Algeria. Yeah, I asked a man for a job and he laughed at me. He said, we hired men over here, we ain't hired no babies. And I just hang around there, you know, every day, and I heard him whispering, you know, say, I'll be that boy that do want to work, you know. Do it up a little bit. He said, that's all right. He said, I believe I'm going to give you a job. Can you roll one of them wheel barrels like you see them fellas doing there? I said, sure, I can do that. I can do anything. He said, well, get your wheel barrel. And I got a wheel barrel that was mixed in concrete up on a, on a mat then. And that's the way they used to mix that stuff, you know. It took a great big fella man with muscles, you know, to turn that stuff over, you know. Well, I couldn't do no mixing but I could roll it after they mixed it up. Man, I was getting all fine at that time. At that time they was paying $2.82 a day from 6 in the morning until 4 in the evening. I used to get my lunch, my cousin would fix my lunch, and I'd go out there and make a day just like the rest of them fellas. So they'd come in. You know fellas play on all jobs, they'd come in to get the kicks out of me, you know. Every time they'd go to mix up a batch of that concrete, I had a way of, I know I was too light, I'd just go sit down and look at them and mix it. When they get through them I'd get my wheel barrel, fall in line and start to, oh, and them fellas used to kid, you know, say, say, boy, you can't sit down on this job. I said, boy, man, see you do that man, see you ain't got no job, you're fired, see you have to get your shovels, help them mix this stuff up, you don't want to get a kick, you know. I'd grab a shovel well in the wake, you know, rolling up on there and couldn't turn it over enough, kick up on the side. So I said, man, you don't mix it that way, you got to have muscle like that and turn it over. And the boss man, I looked around and seen him laughing, you know, he just said, he's killing himself laughing, he turned his back and said, say, fella, come here. I went over there, he said, them fellas try to kid me, he said, they're kidding me, he said, you can't mix that stuff, we got special women to do that, them big fellas there, say, go sit down until they get through. I went and sat down, I was over waking myself, you know, trying to mix that concrete. Say I was wondering, when was the first time you ever?
